World War I (often abbreviated as WWI or WW1), also known as the First World War, the Great War, the Seminal Catastrophe, and initially in North America as the European War, was a global war originating in Europe that lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918. The French Revolution was a period of far-reaching social and political upheaval in France and its colonies beginning in 1789. The Revolution overthrew the monarchy, established a republic, catalyzed violent periods of political turmoil, and finally culminated in a dictatorship under Napoleon who brought many of its principles to areas he conquered in Western Europe and beyond. Inspired by liberal and radical ideas, the Revolution profoundly altered the course of modern history, triggering the global decline of absolute monarchies while replacing them with republics and liberal democracies. Through the Revolutionary Wars, it unleashed a wave of global conflicts that extended from the Caribbean to the Middle East. Historians widely regard the Revolution as one of the most important events in human history.

Bouchon’s loom automated the tedious process of setting up a draw loom using a strip of perforated paper to determine which warp threads had to be raised. As the perforated strip moved forward it acted as a guide so that the machine automatically raised the warp threads to pass the weft through.

The cords of the warp threads were threaded through the eyes of horizontal needles arranged to slide in a box. These needles were either raised or not depending on whether or not there was a perforation in the paper strip at that point. This meant that the perforated strip could be customised. For example, if six needles were placed inside the slide box the individual needles were controlled by six columns of perforations.  If one column had no perforation then only five needles would be raised and one would lay dormant.

A spinning wheel is a device for spinning thread or yarn from fibres.
It was a precursor to later spinning machinery such as the spinning jenny and spinning frame, which displaced the spinning wheel during the Industrial Revolution.
The Spinning Jenny is a multi-spindle spinning frame.

A moving carriage bearing the spindles stretched the thread as it pulled away from the body of the machine, imparting twist to the cotton at the same time. Then the spindles wound up the thread as the carriage returned, before the process started again.
It was simple enough to be operated by a layman or even a strong child, small enough to fit into a farmhouse kitchen and effective enough to revolutionise the production of thread.

It was a sort of half-way house, something to bridge the gap between the spinning wheel and the heavier, more complicated machinery that came later and required factory conditions in which to operate.

It was invented between 1775 and 1779 by Samuel Crompton. The self-acting (automatic) mule was patented by Richard Roberts in 1825.

A power loom is a mechanized loom, and was one of the key developments in the industrialization of weaving during the early Industrial Revolution. A machine which produced twisted threads (initially for warps only), using wooden and metal cylinders rather than human fingers. The spinning frame is an Industrial Revolution invention for spinning thread or yarn from fibres such as wool or cotton in a mechanized way.  
Richard Arkwright employed John Kay to produce a new spinning machine that Kay had worked on with (or possibly stolen from) another inventor called Thomas Highs. The spinning frame was a significant advance over Hargreaves's spinning jenny, in that very little training was required to operate the machinery, which produced a strong yarn suitable for warp threads.

- A cottage industry is an industry—primarily manufacturing—which includes many producers, working from their homes, typically part time. The term originally referred to home workers who were engaged in a task such as sewing, lace-making, wall hangings, electronics, or household manufacturing. Some industries which are usually operated from large, centralized factories were cottage industries before the Industrial Revolution. - Business operators would travel around the world, buying raw materials, delivering them to people who would work on them, and then collecting the finished goods to sell, or typically to ship to another market. - One of the factors which allowed the Industrial Revolution to take place in Western Europe was the presence of these business people who had the ability to expand the scale of their operations. - Cottage industries were very common in the time when a large proportion of the population was engaged in agriculture, because the farmers (and their families) often had both the time and the desire to earn additional income during the part of the year (winter) when there was little work to do farming or selling produce by the farm's roadside

The putting-out system is a means of subcontracting work. Historically, it was also known as the workshop system and the domestic system. In putting-out, work is contracted by a central agent to subcontractors who complete the work in off-site facilities, either in their own homes or in workshops with multiple craftsmen.
The domestic system was suited to pre-urban times because workers did not have to travel from home to work, which was quite impracticable due to the state of roads and footpaths, and members of the household spent many hours in farm or household tasks. Early factory owners sometimes had to build dormitories to house workers, especially girls and women. Putting-out workers had some flexibility to balance farm and household chores with the putting-out work, this being especially important in winter.
At that point, it underwent name and geographical changes. However, bar some technological advancements, the putting-out system has not changed in essential practice. Contemporary examples can be found in China, India, and South America, and are not limited to the textiles industry.

Apostolos Katsikis, emeritus professor of the University of Ioannina, spoke about the history of Kalarrites silversmithing at the Silversmithing Museum event, which was organized by the Cultural Foundation of the Piraeus Group Cultural Foundation in collaboration with the Ephorate of Antiquities of Ioannina and the Patriotic Association of Kalarrites "The Pindos". As Kalarrites, one of the most traditional settlements of Epirus, was once one of the centers of Epirus silversmithing, with famous artisans transferring their creations to large urban centers in Europe. In this village, many pages of the history of silversmithing were written.

Kalarryti silversmithing began to flourish from the 17th century. It is said that the Kalarritines were apprenticed in the silversmithing workshops of Ioannina. They then took the art to their village workshops. They dealt in all kinds of silverware. But they are better known for the ecclesiastical objects they created.

As Mr. Katsikis mentioned, during the period 1750-1850, the most famous silversmith works of modern Greece were created in Kalarryte workshops. Several of the silversmiths were itinerant. Armed only with their work tools, inspiration and unique technique they traveled and fulfilled orders. In this way they saved the art of silversmithing throughout the Balkans, Asia Minor, Egypt, Italy and Austria.

In 1821, the course of Kalarrytine silversmithing was stopped as the settlement was destroyed by the Turks as a reprisal for the rebellion that had broken out in the area. The inhabitants were forced to move to other areas of Epirus, in Thessaly, in the Ionian Islands. And many silversmiths from Kalarrites expanded their business activities in Italy. Characteristic examples, according to Mr. Katsikis, are the Nessi family, still established in Rome, and the Bulgari family ("Bulgari jewelry house"). The silversmiths, far from their place, mutated the traditional technique and created a new "school" in artistic silversmithing. The gospel covers of Athanasios Tzimouris and the reliquary of Agios Dionysios by G. Bafa are considered representative examples of ecclesiastical silversmithing. According to Mr. Katsikis, the creations of these two artisans, as well as many other Kalarrytians, enriched and renewed modern Greek silversmithing.

Tzimouris, a legendary figure for the silversmiths of his time, was born in Kalarrites. After the destruction of the settlement, he settled in Zakynthos where he died in 1823. He worked as chief goldsmith of Ali Pasha and a teacher of silversmithing. His earliest works, works of the continental period, are considered the most important. Always on the covers of the Gospels he created, he carved, as a signature, the phrase: "It was built and is being built in Kalarritais, a village of Ioannina, by the hand of Athanasios Nikolaos Tzimouris".

The second great Kalarritian silversmith was Georgios Bafas, son of Diamantis. He was born in Kalarrites in 1784 and died in Zakynthos in 1854, where his family had settled before the revolution. Baffa's artefacts are many and well-known. From 1812, Bafas worked for the temple of Agios Dionysios and until 1829 he created many works, among others the altar containing the image of the Saint, the patron saint of the island. The reliquary of Saint Dionysios bears the following inscription which confirms the creator and his origin: "On the biennial of the Noble Commissioners Mr. Frantzeskos Montzas, Georgios Komondos and Nikolaos Kandakitis 1829. By hand (Georgiou Diamantis Bafa Kalarytiotou)".

The end for Kalarrites silversmithing came in the first decades of the 20th century, when the circumstances of the time led to the closure of the workshops in Kalarrites. But history was already written in silver letters.

Between 1900 and 1909 the concentration of the Muslim population in the safety of the fortified cities of the island increased, accompanied by the abandonment of rural settlements.

The demographic data from the 'General Census of the Island' in 1900 reflect these processes. The Municipality of Heraklion, the city and its suburbs, numbered 22,481 inhabitants, of whom 11,659 were Muslims and 10,753 were Christians, while 69 "Israelites" should also be taken into account. Muslims still outnumbered Christians in the city, but their proportion in the total population had decreased significantly, a trend that would continue in the following years. The comparison with the 'Census of the population of the island on June 4-5, 1911' reveals the rate of decrease in the Muslim population and, mainly, the reversal of the ratio compared to the Christian population. Out of a total of 25,185 inhabitants of the urban Municipality of Heraklion, Christians were 15,877 and Muslims were only 9,248, while 60 Israelites should be included.

According to N. Andriotis, 'the Muslim population of Crete decreased by half, specifically by 53.7%, from 1881 to 1900, and their percentage of the total population decreased from 25.9% in 1881 to 11% in 1900. The Muslim population of the three major cities decreased by only 13%. In 1900, Muslims still constituted the majority in the cities of Heraklion and Rethymno. However, the Muslim rural population experienced a dramatic decrease, by 83.5%, and went from 18% of the total rural population in 1881 to 2.8% in 1900'.

In addition to the above observations, there is also intense mobility of the Christian populations, who settle in the abandoned rural areas of Heraklion, resulting in population changes. Similar movements, which had already appeared in the previous period, are now occurring with greater intensity, leading to populations from nearby mountainous regions (Lasithi, Sitia) as well as more distant ones (Anogia, Sfakia) settling in the areas abandoned by Muslims, appropriating their properties through purchase or encroachment. It should also be noted that a few Christian families who had left the island for areas within the Greek territory during the turbulent period of the late 19th century have returned.

Another form of mobility that contributes to the demographic changes during this period is "overseas and transcontinental" migration. The insecurity created by difficult economic conditions following long-standing conflicts, exacerbated by the international economic conjuncture, combined with the demand for labor in developing economies in Western Europe and America, leads a significant number of Cretans, both Christians and Muslims, to emigrate abroad. According to Lena Tzedaki-Apostolaki, 'during the first decade of the 20th century, 10,620 people, or 3.5% of the island's population, emigrated from Crete to countries around the world', mainly to Europe and America, and to a lesser extent to Oceania in the case of Christian immigrants, who constitute 70% of the total. It is worth noting that the migration flow to the United States consists almost exclusively of male, and mostly young, population, in contrast to movements to other destinations that often have a family character.

In addition to overseas migration, a new form of mobility emerges during this period, gradually contributing to the formation of the city's population, as well as its social and cultural characteristics. This involves the movement of workers, especially female workers, from the Christian rural populations to the city, on a permanent or seasonal basis, in order to be employed in the already thriving soap industry, but to a large extent in the first raisin processing plants that were being established."

"The city of silversmiths welcomes you", write the signs at the entrances of the city of Ioannina, which, among the many and important elements that make up its cultural identity, chose the "art" of silversmithing to define itself. The centuries-old and timeless tradition of silversmithing in the area, the famous and distinctive works and objects, the schools, the teachers and craftsmen of the same name, but also the modern craftsmen, silversmiths and jewelers, continuers of the tradition, who persist despite the declining dynamics and in bad times to maintain the workshops and the shops with their rich showcases, they give the city its malamatenia glamour.

The history of silversmithing in the region has a long past and is considered a continuation of Byzantine jewelry and metalwork, "arts" that were linked to the church ritual and the needs of the Byzantine Despots for precious metal works. From late Byzantine times, Ioannina, due to their neuralgic position and of the support of the local rulers, they developed, had economic strength and flourished, without being stopped by the Ottoman conquest.In the 17th century there is already evidence of intense activity of the "Kuyoumtzis"(Kouyumtzidon) in a village of Ioannina

During the last decades of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th, the city became the capital of a large and powerful palace to develop into an important commercial and industrial center. The conditions further favored the cultivation of silversmithing, which flourished. Ali Pasha himself, not only was a collector of valuable objects himself, but he founded at that time silversmithing workshops inside the palace and gathered the best craftsmen in them. During the period of Ali (1788-1822) the artisans numbered 55, while their works were promoted not only in the internal market, but in the European West, and in the Balkan world of the Ottoman Empire.

Beyond Ioannina, however, the art also flourished in other silversmithing centers of Epirus, such as Kalarrites (Tzoumerka), Konitsa, Metsovo, Zagori, Arta, etc. Especially the silversmiths of Kalarry, under the patronage of Ali Pasha, gave a special impetus to the art. Leading masters of the "Malamo-smoked" or "Savatlid style", who left behind a brilliant legacy, were the first who, knowing their value, numbered and signed their works with their name and place of origin. The signature of the chief goldsmith and master of silversmithing in the court of Ali, Athanasios Tzimouris on a gospel cover is characteristic: "It was made and is being made in Kallarites, a village of Ioannina by the hand of Athanasios Tzimouris". After all, the Bulgarians of the now famous Bulgari house, which has been active since the 19th century in Italy, were also from Kalarryti.

The predominant and even exclusively used metal was silver even in the most expensive commissions of precious works from powerful religious centers. Pure silver was reserved for the finest works, the "lagara". Next, the poorest in grades: good and ordinary. Gold and silver were the same for the common craftsman. Both they and the ordinary people used the word gold to describe both malama (gold) and silver. Hence the artisans, in addition to silversmiths, were also called goldsmiths.

In the works, ecclesiastical (chalices, reliquaries, silver-plated crosses, coverings of gospels, censers, etc.) and secular (jewelry, utensils, items for personal use, weapons, etc.), all known techniques were applied: engraved, printed or blown , wire or filigree, perforated or serrated, savat, cast, enamelled. Often two and three techniques coexist.

Until the first decades of the 20th century, the master, the complete craftsman, possessed all the techniques and participated in all phases of the production process. Knowledge and practical training required discipline, labor and many years of hard apprenticeship. Only in this way could one bear the "title" of "master" who enjoyed great social recognition, acclaim and fame. In the following years, up to the present day, the artisans specialized both in terms of technology and in terms of knowledge and the organization of production.

Silversmithing is today one of the few remaining living branches of traditional Greek folk art that has ongoing and produced works. During a short tour of the Center for Traditional Crafts (KEPAVI), on the lakefront of the city, where since 2005 silversmithing workshops and the Silver Retail Shop have been operating, I was informed by Mr. Phaedon Ilias, president of the Ioannina Silversmiths' Association "I Gianniotiki Techni" , that today there are about 100 laboratories in the city (from 1960 to 1980 there were around 300), while within the facilities of KEPAVI - although there is infrastructure for 60 laboratories - only 20 are operating. Even the rent of 150 euros, in crisis conditions, is unaffordable for the city's artisans, who have been affected in recent decades, especially since 1990 and since, due to the opening of the markets, the numerous and uncontrolled imports, but also the incessant copying and usurping their traditional designs and decorative motifs, which came to be "reproduced as far away as China even in pencil."

Asking Mr. Ilias from whom he learned the "art" he answered "from my father". Indeed, technical knowledge and training is passed down from father to son, through the generations, in an unbroken historical sequence. There are no vocational schools. However, the continuation and development of silversmithing in Ioannina in the 20th century is largely due, beyond the craftsmen's workshops that previously provided practical training and knowledge to the apprentice or work to the semi-skilled craftsman, to the establishment and operation of the Georgiou Stavros School of Silversmithing from 1930 to 1940, and those who succeeded her afterwards.In 1959 the School was founded which was expanded by the National Organization of Greek Handicrafts and then (from 1975) supervised by the OAED. Mr. Ilias's father also graduated from there, as did other silversmiths of the city, who today pass on the tradition and technical experience to the younger generation. In a crisis like the one we are experiencing in Greece in recent years, vocational schools and the turning of young people into productive professions are in demand. Especially when we are talking about the future of a living - and not just a museum - branch, such as silversmithing, which has a special identity, a centuries-old past, and must have a future as well.

In the castle of Ioannina, in Its Kale (inner citadel) is the "Treasury" (an annex of the Byzantine Museum), where an exhibition of silversmithing is housed, which includes two main collections of silver objects, which are donations of Archbishop Spyridon (1873-1956). and K. Ioannidis (son of a well-known family of silversmiths, 1907-1965).Recently, the exhibition has been enriched by the donation of precious jewels and other objects. In the objects exhibited here, ecclesiastical and secular, the skill of the continental silversmiths in all types of silversmithing, as well as in all techniques, can be seen in relief. The exhibition is complemented by a silversmithing workshop, which was set up with the help of the Silversmiths' Association of Ioannina.

Last July, the Municipality of Ioannina in collaboration with the Metropolis of Ioannina, the support of the Region of Epirus, the cooperation of the 8th Ephorate of Byzantine Antiquities and KEPAVI, as well as the participation of private individuals and institutions, organized an exhibition with title: "The silver art of the Ioannina. Silversmithing in Ioannina through the ages", which was inaugurated on 15/7 at the Museum-Exhibition Complex of the Moscow Region "New Jerusalem". The exhibition was not only warmly received (5000 visitors by September 1st), but a request was made for its two-month extension. Therefore, the relevant entities are thinking of touring to other European countries. It is the first time that the city authorities took an extroverted initiative in relation to silversmithing, a fact that cannot but strengthen and highlight its cultural profile, reawakening interest in its tradition, present and future silversmithing, to boost tourism and its battered local market everywhere. The reputation of Ioannina silversmithing "raises" extroversion, participation in international exhibitions, mobility, creation with a future.

On July 26, 1896, the Revolutionary Assembly was formed in Tzitzifes, Apokoronas, resulting in a resolution submitted to the consuls. This event officially denoted the renunciation of the Sultan's authority. After the intervention of the Great Powers, the following requests of the revolutionaries were accepted: the appointment of a Christian governor and Christian officials in a two-thirds ratio, the convening of the Assembly every two years, the right of Cretans to vote on the budget and laws, the reorganization of the rural police and the courts.

This resulted in the Great Powers sending an international force and proceeding with the division of the island into occupation zones. The British occupied Heraklion, the Russians took Rethymno, the Italians took Chania, the French took Sitia, the Germans took Souda, and the Austrians took Kíssamos.

The Treaty of Constantinople (December 4, 1897) granted autonomy to Crete. Various names were proposed for the position of the General Governor, and finally, Prince George, the second son of the then King of Greece, was chosen. An elected executive committee, including Eleftherios Venizelos, temporarily executed the duties of the government and established contacts with the Great Powers. Muslim inhabitants of Crete were in turmoil, while Christians also formed armed groups. Eventually, control of the countryside was regained by the Christians, while the Muslims sought refuge in the cities.
Archaeological evidence suggests that the first true synthetic glass was made in Lebanon and the coastal north Syria, Mesopotamia or ancient Egypt.

If the knowledge of glass art in the High Middle Ages remains relatively fragmentary, the activity develops from the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The great abbeys, anxious to enhance their domains, encouraged the construction
of glassworks. Aware of the economic interest represented by these establishments, the Dukes of Lorraine took them under their protection. Thus, in 1448, Jean de Calabria, governor of Lorraine, granted them the famous Charter of Glassmakers, assimilating them to nobility with the title of squire and thereby granting them numerous privileges. In a region rich in raw materials – the thick coat of sandstone provides the silica and the vast forest massif provides the wood needed to heat the ovens – the glass industry prospers and the quality of the productions is underlined by many authors.

Fearing the total disappearance of glassmaking activity on its territory, the ducal government welcomes foreign glassmakers. They settled on the northeastern borders of the duchy, whether it was the country of Bitche, the lower Saar near Creutzwald and Merlebach or the upper Saar, in other words, Saint-Quirin and the Sarrebourg region.

The dawn of the 18th century coincided in Lorraine with the beginning of a long period of peace and favourable opportunities for the economic development of the region.  The glass sector is experiencing a new boom. Many glassworks are founded. They are generally established for longer periods than in the past when moving according to timber concessions, they were nicknamed “flying glassworks”. Some of these establishments achieve notoriety and contributed to the reputation of the Lorraine glass industry. Let us mention Meisenthal in 1704, Portieux in 1705, Plaine-de-Walsch which gave birth to Vallérysthal in 1707, Saint-Quirin in 1737, Baccarat in 1764, Vannes-le-Châtel 1765, and Saint-Louis at 1767.

Most glassworks have a varied production and simultaneously manufacture gobletware, but also flat glass, and sometimes also bottles and watch glasses. Over time, however, glassware tends to become predominant. Glasses became habitual ornaments of noble and bourgeois tables. Their size and shape vary depending on the content they are intended to receive. A number of establishments are also trying to imitate "flint glass", the crystal developed by the Englishman Ravenscroft in 1674. Saint-Louis succeeded in this as early as 1781.

The nineteenth century of the industrial revolution marked the glass sector by the importance of progress favouring mass production. The glassmakers partly renounce their empiricism and ask science for the means that they lacked until then. Chemistry and technology play a key role in this progress. If in the field of bottling and flat glass, progress is considerable, they are no less numerous in that of glassware: compressed air, pressure moulding, improvement in the quality of white glass, and development of new enamelling and lining techniques.

This creative bubbling and the considerable technical progress experienced by the glass industry were stimulated by the general economic development allowing the bourgeoisie to acquire quality products to furnish their sumptuous residences. If the Universal Exhibitions are an opportunity for craftsmen to be in the spotlight, they also offer supporters of Art Nouveau the names attached to this period, let us mention Gallé, Daum – who collaborated with artists such as Jacques Gruber, Henri Bergé and Amalric Walter – or the Muller brothers.

At the turn of the 20th century, rich in their traditional know-how and ability to adapt, Lorraine manufactures ran at full speed. In 1900, Baccarat employed 2,400 workers, and Saint-Louis exceeded 2,000. New establishments were founded.
But this golden age was not long in coming to an end: the stock market crash of 1929 and the social movements of the 1930s, then the Second World War marked ruptures

After the prosperous period of the Glorious Thirties, at the end of the 1980s and especially during the 1990s, the luxury industries were faced with great difficulties linked to the evolution of purchasing habits and in particular the decline of the share represented by tableware in wedding lists.

As in the past, businesses need to be adaptable to stay competitive and, above all, accommodate technical advancements, even in traditional operations. The whole difficulty lies in the need to find the right balance between this trend towards mechanization and the preservation of the artisanal character, presented as a guarantee of quality. Creation is given special attention.

Today, the Grand Est still brings together the big names of the French crystal factory. It also hosts international industrial glass companies, both in the field of bottle-making than flat glass or even optical glass. We must also add a multitude of workshops artisanal, using traditional techniques or innovative, disseminated throughout the territory.

The Pact of Halepa (Greek: Σύμβαση της Χαλέπας) or Halepa Charter (Χάρτης της Χαλέπας) was an agreement made in 1878 between the Ottoman Empire (then ruled by the Sultan Abdul Hamid II) and the representatives of the Cretan Revolutionary Committee, which secured wide-ranging autonomy for the island of Crete. It was named after the place where it was signed, Halepa (now a district of Chania).

The revolution of 1889 became the reason for the limitation of the privileges granted by the Treaty of Halepa by the Ottoman Empire. The policing of the island was assigned to Ottoman forces from Macedonia, and the suppression of the revolution was followed by extensive massacres of Christians, desecrations, and the destruction of churches.

However, the concentration of powers in the hands of the prince in the areas of executive and legislative authority, as well as his often autocratic manner of exercising his duties, caused serious problems from the beginning. These issues included the restriction of the Assembly's powers and the unclear definition of the authorities of the institutions of the Cretan State. In these circumstances, frequent interventions in administration were observed, political dialogue was essentially abolished, municipal officials were appointed by central authority, and newspaper circulation was often prohibited. Moreover, staffing the government apparatus with experienced officials from the Greek state contributed to the effective exclusion of Cretans from making significant political and administrative decisions. Lastly, the endeavor of economic reconstruction proved difficult despite a loan of 4,000,000 francs, secured with the guarantee of the Protecting Powers.
These phenomena escalated the dissatisfaction of the population, which, despite the complexity of the project, continued to view union with Greece as the only way out. The relationship between Prince George and Eleftherios Venizelos also proved challenging. Their disagreements were frequent and intense, most notably regarding the policy to be pursued on the Union issue.

About 250 years ago, the so-called Vannes-le-Châtel glassworks was created, although it is located on the territory of the commune of Allamps, which was then part of the seigneury of Vannes. Indeed, in 1765, Madame de Reims (or de Rheims, according to the writings), born Marie-Anne Gabrielle Roze de Barbarat de Mazirot, wife of Antoine Bernard de Reims, lord of Vannes, built the first glass factory. Its goal: to use the products of its immense forests which it wanted to promote by manufacturing glasses and so-called gobletware objects, a booming market.

The Reims family received the seigneury of Vannes around 1724, certainly by purchase from the Ligniville family ( today we would write Lignéville). It then passed into the hands of Laurent Hocquet de Saint Léger before 1779.

It was sold shortly afterwards, in 1788; Louis Nicolas Griveau, king's adviser, notary, acquires the Vannes estate. He lived there during the Revolution, thus avoiding Paris. He became a member of the general council of the department of Meurthe, then deputy. He died on October 20, 1823 in Vannes.

All of these successive owners do not report any particular skills in the glass trades. We can think that they act more as investors and for the development of their territory, than as industrialists. However, from 1796, the management of the factory was entrusted to tradespeople, the Sieurs Schmid, renowned master glassmakers whose ancestors were present in a large number of glassworks in eastern France . Links will continue to be forged in the 20th century between the directing families of these great glassworks.

The development really started after the Schmid family took ownership of the glassworks in 1827.The factory employs around a hundred craftsmen and laborers who are "slaves" to the glass melting furnace. Indeed, wood fusion is then an uncontrolled process. Staff must be available when the glass is ready to be “picked1". A bell announces the start of work according to the vagaries of glass melting, at any time of day or night. This system works before a better mastery of fusion thanks to the heating of coal furnaces in 1870.

But before this innovation, several investments contributed to the development of glassmaking: the construction of a water cutting plant in 1846, then the installation of a first press and an acid etching workshop around 1880. If  although the workforce of the glassworks reached more than 400 employees in 1884.

As M. The death of Ernest Schmid in 1908 marked the end of the "Schmid" dynasty. It was Albert Bourbonneux, his son-in-law, who became manager on behalf of the company Les enfants d'Ernest Schmid. This direction opens a new industrial era.

From 1908 to 1945, the factory produced increasingly fine articles to fight against foreign competition. Between the two wars, through family ties, the glass works of Vannes were united for a time with the Société des verreries de Vierzon.


Albert died in 1937. Two of his sons, François-Joseph Marie and Marie-Joseph Michel Claude, took over from him . The Second World War arrives in 1939. Then, the glass claims its place and its recognition!
The very words of the glassmakers bear witness to this. They evoke it with a form of respect, like that of a mysterious master , as if it were a person. Then their tricks do the rest of the magic to seduce us. "We have to respect it," they say. The glass does not rush, it is he who decides, you have to remain humble with him. And especially the key phrase heard a thousand times: “We learn something every day with this material! The momentum and popular solidarity are then reinforced . Little by little, the hard work of those who get up early, who go from their workers' housing estate to the "Grand'Place" with their flashlights, haversacks on their backs, husband and wife on duty, is forgotten. Subjugated life is organized around the factory.

Glass invites, outside the working conditions of another century, to dream, to perpetuated tradition, to beauty, to the nobility of luxury, of which we know nothing here, and it regales us with mysteries. From the creation of Cerfav,
in contact with the first visual artists we met, we learn that it traps a number of artists. Believing to use it, they finally feel deprived of all merit as it imposes itself by the power of its aspects. The brilliance, the transparency, the radiance, the effects of materials amaze spontaneously. "The viewer makes the work", instructed us Marcel Duchamp, but then where did the author go? The glass catches the light, risking relegating the artistic message
to the rank of anecdote.

Scientists also wonder a lot about the enigmas it poses. Indeed, his behavior often puts their knowledge to the test. We must not rely on the appearances it gives: glass shuffles the cards into tales, both counter truths and scientific assertions, however solid they may seem. While it is certainly the oldest synthetic material exploited by man, we are constantly discovering it and finding new applications for it in unexpected fields.

Throughout history, it has allowed polychrome stained glass windows in cathedrals; it illustrates the apogee of Venice through excellence and finesse. The crystal, first discovered in England, later arrived in Lorraine, where the crystal works became a benchmark in the tableware, luxury, jewelery and lighting industries. Today, glass is ultra-contemporary, in the plastic arts of course, and we also note its use in electronics, optics, telecommunications, construction, health, aeronautics, nuclear, automotive, energy, medical. It could well, by the way, constitute a technical solution to automotive batteries!

The 20th Century is a period of disruption, where the tapestry reinforces its link with the avant-garde creation. Some institutions such as the Aubusson National School of Decorative Arts and personalities like Antoine-Marius Martin (School’s director) , Marie Cuttoli (collector and textile editor), play here a leading role. But history remembers mostly one name: the painter Jean Lurçat, founder of the tapestry renewal from the 1940’s onwards.
Aubusson’s National School of Decorative Arts

In 1884, Aubusson’s municipal drawing School, founded in the 18th Century (in the move of the royal tapestry Manufacture reform), becomes the National School of Decorative Arts, beside Paris’ and Limoges’, with the same director Auguste Louvrier de Lajolais (1829-1908). The latter relies on professors from Paris to supply both provincial cities with models.

The School, so called “ENAD” in French (Ecole Nationale d’Arts Décoratifs), plays an important part in the renewal of the tapestry art and technique in the 20th Century. The School dispenses courses of low- and high-warp weaving and “Saracen” embroidery, known under the name of Aubusson cross stitch embroidery. Well-known artists furnishes cartoons: Pierre-Victor Galland (1822-1892) , painter decorator; Charles Genuys  (1852-1928), chief architect of the historical monuments; Henry de Waroquier (1881-1970), painter and engraver, professor at the Estienne School in Paris.

From 1917, the Aubusson School’s new director, Antoine-Marius Martin (1869-1955) wishes to see the art of weaving evolve.

- Renew the models by looking for different painters of his era, notably postimpressionists;

- Retain in the medieval tapestries, characteristics transposable to the modernity: reduce the amount of colors, weave with much larger threads, use a more assertive technical writing (battage, stripes, piping etc.)

He replaces painted cartoons (models for the weavers) by inked cartoons, so-called “à tons comptés”, which are now drawings with its lines marking out the divers colored surfaces.

Then, very early, he would theorize and publish the principles of what he calls the tapestry Renovation twenty years before the artist Jean Lurçat, considered since the 1940’s as the inventor of this Renovation.

In 1925, Antoine-Marius Martin, Aubusson School’s director, presents his researches of the tapestry renewal on a stand at the Grand Palais during the prestigious international Exhibit of Decorative Arts. The public discovers there totally unreleased student works and is amazed by the thickness of the used threads but catch a glimpse of the modernity of these young creations as well.

Antoine-Marius Martin’s successor, Elie Maingonnat (1892-1966) pursues until 1958 the same dynamic, with the artist Jean Lurçat and his followers, from 1937 onwards.

The new conducted researches within the Aubusson National School of Decorative Arts during the 1920’s lead to a painter’s movement knowing the tapestry techniques and are the authors of their own weaving-suitable cartoons. Thus, the textile interpretation, basis of the art of tapestry making, is here strongly mastered by the artist.

In the early 20th Century, Jean Lurçat is an artist linked with the surrealist movement. His painting encounters a pretty good success, his mother and his first wife (Marthe Hennebert) realize for him massive needlestitch tapestries.

For the editor and collector Marie Cuttoli, he draws rugs and a first cartoon of tapestry is weaved in Aubusson in 1931. In 1937, he discovers the innovative work of the Aubusson National School of Decorative Arts, so as the 16th Century hanging, so-called “d’Anglards-de-Salers”, which makes a strong impression on him. The following year, he is deeply marked by the Apocalypse hanging in Angers. In 1939, the national Manufactures’ director, Guillaume Jeanneau, entrusts him with the order of a furniture ensemble with tapestry (weaved at the Gobelins) and a mission in Aubusson: find a new genre of decor. The models created are remarked thanks to the strength of their expressivity and their few vivid colors.

Jean Lurçat is a great actor of the tapestry renewal in the 20th Century. He played a particularly important role due to the amount of orders he provoked, contributing to a workshop boost and many hiring (Dom Robert, Marc Saint-Saëns, Mario Prassinos, Robert Wogensky, Michel Tourlière, Mathieu Matégot etc.), creating a very strong emulation in Aubusson.

His tapestries with vivid colors have most of the time a monumental character destined to dress up modern architectures. His symbolic universe plays over the four elements, the vegetal and animal kingdom, the human’s place in the cosmos. The artist puts into frame poetic writings (of Eluard, Aragon, Tzara, Desnos etc.) and claims in his weavings the engagement in the Second World War Resistance. His graphics is characteristic and some motives such as the sun and the rooster are key symbols.

Marie Cuttoli (1879-1973) is a woman with a strong personality, Avant-garde works collector in the beginning of the 20th Century, tapestry lover and art seller. She does not have any interest in the “official” artists of the Aubusson National School of Decorative Arts. She took advantage of her husband’s (Paul Cuttoli) nomination as prefect of Algeria to settle down there a rug manufacture, Myrbor. She entrusts the models creation to contemporary artists (Fernand Léger, Jean Lurçat).

From 1928 onwards, she had Aubusson tapestries done by placing an order to several artists: Lucien Couteau, Jean Lurçat, Georges Rouault, Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, Le Corbusier, Raoul Dufy, Man Ray etc. She had notably the Marcelle Delarbre workshop in Aubusson working. The weavings went immediately to her Parisian collection or to the USA, where she organized in 1939 an important touring exhibition with help of the collector Albert Barnes and the San Fransisco museum conservator. This exhibition and its escorting catalogs will develop an American customer base, acquainted with the French Avant-garde painter’s tapestry style. The impact is so big that even today, in the USA; “aubusson” is still used as a common name to qualify a low-pile carpet.

There is a second stream, which marks the 20th Century, with some artists having tapestries occasionally weaved and who bound, if needed, with a cartoon painter made responsible for the adaptation of their original work to the tapestry of Aubusson weaving style.

Pierre Baudoin (1921-1970) is an artist teaching at Aubusson’s and Paris’ Sèvres highschool. In 1946, he discovers the tapestry and falls in love with the question of the textile transcription of an art work, whose first purpose is not to become weaved. He becomes a specialist in this field as he developed tapestry cartoons from original works (often etching or small size paintings). He chooses the weavings’ texture (size of the stitch) and manages the wool dying.

He works at first with Henri-Georges Adam, then for Le Corbusier, of who he would become the assistant in the realization of weaved works. He develops cartoons for George Braque, Alexandre Calder, Jean Arp, Pablo Picasso, André Beaudin, Max Ernst, Maurice Estève, Charles Lapicque etc. The weavings are subtle and relevant transpositions. Thanks to the intelligence and the accuracy of Pierre Baudoin’s adaptation work, the artists were always fully authors of their works weaved.

In 1951, Denise René, gallery owner in Paris, specialized in abstract and optical art, begins to edit tapestries with the will to create previously unseen and experimental pieces. To produce these new works, she gets in touch with François Tabard, head of one of the most important tapestry workshop in Aubusson.

The kingpin of this adventure is Victor Vasarely, optical art painter. He establishes for himself and for the artists the cartoons from original templates using the technique of the enlarged photograph.

The regular artists of the gallery are Dewasne, Deyrolle, Herbin, Magnelli, Mortensen, Pillet and Vasarely, associated with celebrities such as Arp, Taeuber Arp, Kandinsky, Léger and Le Corbusier. After a first exhibition in June 1952, many others take place in Paris or New York, including new artists as well, such as Albers, Agam, Sonia Delaunay, Van Doesburg, Bloc etc. The abstract tapestry knew at that time its full development.

In 1960, Pierre Baudoin (cartoon painter) and Jacques Lagrange (artist) organize an exhibition of Coptic tapestries, lent notably by the Louvres museum, to the “Galerie d’Aubusson (Grenelle street in Paris) with André de Persine, landlord.

Struck by the plastic art power emanating from these small formats, they convinced several artists to create small size projects: Arp, Braque, Calder, Edelmann, Gischia, Lagrange, Picasso etc.

The weavings of these small size formats began from 1960 onwards. They are technically demanding, because at that scale, even the smallest flaw can be visible.

In the late 1960’s, Michel Tourlière (1925-2004) have the actual building of Aubusson’s NSDA built, with the project of creating an institution based on the excellence of the weaver’s formation and a vast opening worldwide. In the 1960’s, merged with the one of Limoges, Aubusson’s NSDA engages within the scope of creative school’s European competition, as the perspective of textile design as a possible evolution of the tapestry teaching was not retained. Thereafter, the educational resources are transferred to Limoges, leading to the unavoidable closing down of the establishment. The building encounters today a new lease of life thanks to the creation of the “Cité internationale de la tapisserie.”

The Egyptians made kilns to place their clay pots in for firing. The kiln was lined with a kind of insulation brick that was made from a mixture of straw and clay which had been dried in the sun. Further experimentation lead the Egyptians to coat their clay objects with a bluish-green substance to make them non-porous. This was a glaze composed of quartz, soda, and a mineral containing copper which when fired covered the clay bowls and vases with a glass-like surface.

In medieval times sand was mixed with clay to make cooking pots strong enough to be placed over an open fire. Today, for the same reason, casseroles used for baking are made from clay mixed with grog which is a ground-up fired pottery. The openness of grog clay allows water to evaporate more evenly as it dries and prevents cracking and warping during the firing. Grog clay eases the problem of heat expansion which can cause large thick pieces of pottery or sculpture to blow up in the kiln.

The finest achievements came in the Late Minoan period, pieces of which were widely exported around the Aegean civilizations and sometimes beyond, and are the high points of the Minoan pottery tradition.

Little is known about the way the pottery was produced, but it was probably in small artisanal workshops, often clustered in settlements near good sources of clay for potting. For many, potting may well have been a seasonal activity, combined with farming, although the volume and sophistication of later wares suggests full-time specialists, and two classes of workshop, one catering to the palaces.

Around 1450 BCE, the Mycenaean Greeks must have moved into the palace of Knossos. They were well-established by 1400, if the Linear B tablets can be dated to then. The resulting culture is not a break with the Minoan past. Minoan traditions continue under a new administration. However, the vase forms and designs became more and more Mycenaean in character with a large variety of decoration. Style names have multiplied and depend to some degree on the author. The designs are found also on seals and ceilings, in frescoes and on other artefacts. Often Late Minoan pottery is not easily placed in sub-periods. In addition are imports from the neighbouring coasts of the Mediterranean.

During the classical and Hellenistic Periods (480 BCE - 67 BCE), pottery production in Crete continued, albeit with a shift in styles. The influence of Athenian pottery became prominent, as Cretan potters adopted red-figure and black-figure techniques. The subjects depicted on the pottery ranged from mythological scenes to daily life activities.

In the Roman and Byzantine Periods (67 BCE - 9th century CE),, the local pottery industry flourished. Roman pottery styles, such as terra sigillata (red gloss ware), were produced on the island. During the Byzantine period, in the 10th-12th century, rural pottery was locally produced and similar to that of previous centuries, with the increasingly common appearance of glazed ware imported from Byzantium with the characteristic decoration of the time. During the 12th century, Cretan biscuit ware (pottery that has been fired once but not glazed) was refined and certain forms emulated Aegean prototypes widely circulating in the Byzantine Empire.  At the same time, locally-produced open glazed vessels with a short wide foot appeared, in monochrome dark brown or dark green. These probably had a ritual function, as their sherds are found in the environs of old churches.
During the Venetian Occupation, 1205-1645, in the first period of intense hostilities (1205-1300), pottery production fell or remained stationary.

During the second period (1300-1460), ending with the fall of Constantinople to the Turks, local production diversified into a wide variety of forms and decoration. Small biscuit ware vessels began to be decorated with applied clay colouring (slip), shading from red to dark brown depending on the firing. The decoration was particularly simple, consisting of parallel lines, cross hatching etc. Large biscuit ware vessels such as storage jars, basins, beehives, troughs etc. began to come in various shapes and sizes decorated with incised or stamped designs. During this period, Cretan glazed ware appeared and flourished. This included plates, bowls, jugs etc., in soft, delicate shades of green and yellow, or with brown spots on a white background. Domestic ware was decorated with geometric patterns, spirals, flower petals etc. This decoration was applied by delicate incision of the vessel, over the slip and colour, which darkened after firing. The decoration of Cretan glazed ware differs from that found in the Peloponnese, Cyprus and Asia Minor.

The third period (1460-1645) was distinguished by a major resurgence in pottery production during the first phase to 1550. The large forms, mainly storage jars, were often decorated using cylinder seals, which were rolled around the vessel to produce decorative bands. The variety of glazed ware increased and the vessels were distributed widely through the countryside, with a corresponding steady improvement of quality. During the second phase (1550-1645) pottery, and especially glazed ware, began to decline. Incised decoration was simplified or even vanished entirely, while coloured decoration became softer and spread across the whole surface. This decline is probably due to the widespread insecurity of the Venetian Dominions following the fall of Cyprus to the Turks (1570) and the Ottoman advance.

In the Ottoman Rule and Modern Times (1669 CE - Present), production in Crete declined significantly. However, traditional Cretan pottery continued to be made in small workshops, primarily for household purposes. The pottery was often characterised by its simplicity and earthy tones. In the 20th century, there was a revival of interest in Cretan pottery, with artisans incorporating traditional techniques and designs into their work.

During the first phase of the Turkish Occupation, 1645-1898, biscuit ware with clay slip continued to be used, but glazed ware became rarer and coloured exclusively a light green. At the same time, characteristic two-coloured plates were imported from Rhodes. The larger vessels, particularly storage jars, continued to flourish due to the high production of olive oil during the 18th century. However, their decoration too was reduced.

During the second phase of the Turkish Occupation (1770-1898), the constant armed Cretan risings against the Turks created deep social and financial insecurity. All types of production were drastically reduced and limited to essentials necessary to survival. Glazed ware was no longer produced and all other types of pottery were only present in their simplest forms.

Four Pottery Centres were established in Crete at the beginning of the second millennium, one in each prefecture. The reasons for this distribution and choice of location are not known, as there are rich sources of clay everywhere in Crete.

The Pottery Centres were villages where only part of the population was involved in ceramics, while the profession did not necessarily pass exclusively from father to son. Potters and Cretans in general considered it to be one of the worst crafts to exercise, due to the constant exposure to mud and the low income.

Potters were divided into specialist pithos makers or pitharades and those who produced smaller shapes. Their indispensable assistants were the clay digger (homatas), who recognised and excavated the layers of clay, and the kiln minder (kaminiaris) who regulated the kiln heat during the firing of the pots. This was a great responsibility, as traditional kilns had no thermometers or heat gauges and any mistake during the 10-12 hours of firing meant that the whole batch would be ruined.

In the two larger Pottery Centres the potters formed guilds, small groups of six known as takimi who scattered across the whole island from April to September. Each group would work for the whole period in a specific countryside location with a source of clay, water and a kiln, away from any villages. The seasonal migration of the guild group was called the vendema (Italian for vintage or harvest), because each year the potters chose an area where there would be a good olive harvest (vendema) and therefore the growers would need pithoi, the most lucrative type of ceramic to make.

The location of a suitable worksite for the group each year was undertaken by the mastoras in the winter. He would travel to different areas of Crete looking for places where there would be a good olive harvest the following autumn, bearing in mind that olive trees bear fruit every two years.

Once a suitable spot was found, he had to rent a kiln from its owner. There was a special tradition for this in Crete. Let’s say that a group has found a suitable site but there is no kiln. The mastoras chooses a spot near a clay deposit, a water source and on ground suitable to build a kiln, which is usually quite large. He negotiates permission to build the kiln with the owner of the land, and comes back with his group in the early spring to construct it, in two to three weeks. The kiln then becomes the property of the farmer on whose land it is. He rents it to the group who built it or other potters each year. Thus the kilns of the migratory groups belong to the owners of the land rather than the potters. Over the years, many kilns were built across Crete and the guild groups had little difficulty in finding and using this essential structure.

World War II (often abbreviated to WWII or WW2), also known as the Second World War, was a global war that lasted from 1939 to 1945. The vast majority of the world's countries—including all the great powers—eventually formed two opposing military alliances: the Allies and the Axis. A state of total war emerged, directly involving more than 100 million people from more than 30 countries. The major participants threw their entire economic, industrial, and scientific capabilities behind the war effort, blurring the distinction between civilian and military resources. World War II was the deadliest conflict in human history, marked by 70 to 85 million fatalities, most of whom were civilians in the Soviet Union and China. It included massacres, the genocide of the Holocaust, strategic bombing, premeditated death from starvation and disease, and the only use of nuclear weapons in war.

The Archaeological Museum of Heraklion, the largest museum for the Minoan culture in Greece and in the world, apart from the diverse forms of life and Minoan art it displays, also occupies a prominent position in the world history of weaving. Minoan textiles are amazing in their design complexity, with geometric shapes and motifs mostly from the natural world. Equally complex and elegant are the garments familiar to us from many categories of sources. The most important are the representations of human figures in the well-known frescoes of Knossos which date mainly to the neo-palatial period. Processions and elaborate cult scenes are depicted. Garments of exceptional art are represented, elegant in their details, bodices, skirts, tunics, The Sacred Knot, a wide band tied in a knot and attached to the neck, deserves special mention. The color scale exploits the contrasts of the exposed tapes with the colorful or simple main parts of the garments. In terms of clothing representations of equal importance are seals and seals with all kinds of cult scenes and elaborate costumes. Rituals are also witnessed around the dedication of garments that are formally carried and hung on short ones.

The Heraklion Museum preserves remains of two important functions: of spinning, which is done with the help of a spindle, to make thread, of which only the flywheels have been preserved, and secondly of weaving, specifically the agnythes, remains of the loom with weights, where the weaving was done . The agnyths were the weights that stretched the warps.

In this exhibition, a reconstruction of the weight loom is made.

It was a great effort, where a carpenter, an archaeologist and a skilled weaver collaborated, in long hours of meetings and a series of tests, to achieve the operation of the loom in the ancient way. Minoan textiles were also woven with their motifs especially for this exhibition and with threads produced like the ancient ones and displayed next to the ancient loom. Finally, the agnyths hanging from the warps are genuine copies of the ancient ones.

In the museum of Heraklion there is another category of finds connected to the production of textiles. They are the Linear B tablets that record information about the production, types and trade of textiles, which was of great importance for the development of the Minoan civilization.

From 1940 onwards, a harsh economic situation was experienced, which worsened in 1948, affecting both the industry and the population due to job losses and the industry's difficult survival. In this context, the parish priest and Archpriest of the New Church "La Purísima", José Esteban Díaz, who was also a regional delegate for trade unions, proposed at the end of 1948 the creation of an Industrial Cooperative to alleviate the situation faced by workers. He founded the COMED (Cooperative Worker of Furniture Esteban Díaz). However, it was inaugurated after his death, but for years it was the most important company in Yecla with over 150 workers and a modern factory. This led to a large number of employees creating their own furniture sector businesses. Most scholars assert that José Esteban Díaz represented the seed of Yecla's industrialization..

José Antonio López Palao was born in Yecla and in his youth worked as a carpenter in the "Santos Nuevos" workshop, where he seems to have developed a great passion for carving and sculpture. At the age of 19 or 20, he enrolled in the San Carlos School of Fine Arts in Valencia. Upon completing his studies, he set up a workshop in Valencia, where he produced most of his work and honed his artistic skills and quality. Although he frequently stayed in Yecla, where he had a small workshop, it was in 1932, at the age of 67, that he settled permanently in his hometown until his death. His works were abundant, and some studies done at the academy as well as several busts are preserved. Among his many notable pieces are the old throne of the Virgin (1917), the Virgin of the Three Hail Marys, and a Christ of Mercy.

In 1961, fifteen furniture factories decided to hold the Local Furniture Exhibition at the Colegio de los Padres Escolapios in the city. The success of this initiative led to the first official edition being held a year later under the name “Provincial Furniture and Related Industries Fair”. At this exhibition, 24 companies displayed their products across 43 stands in a space of 700 square metres. These beginnings highlighted Yecla and placed the industry on the map, driving economic and socio-cultural development in Yecla, which becomes evident with each passing edition.

Starting from 1940, a severe economic situation emerged, which worsened in 1948, affecting both the industry and the population due to job losses and the difficult survival of the industry. In this context, the archpriest José Esteban Díaz, who was also the regional delegate of trade unions, found an opportunity amid this crisis by creating an industrial cooperative in 1949.

Since 1995 Furniture and Wood Technology Centre of the Region of Murcia (CETEM) has organised the International Industrial Design Competition for Furniture to promote innovation. Its main objectives are to encourage collaboration between companies and designers and to promote a design culture as a strategy for competitiveness and differentiation.
Any national or international designer, both individually or as a group, or any manufacturer from the habitat sector can take part.

The Furniture and Wood Technology Centre of the Region (CETEM) and the University of Murcia (UMU) created the Master's degree in 'Design and Industrial Organisation for the Furniture and Wood Sector’. This course has its roots in a degree programme of the same name, initiated in 1997, also in collaboration with CETEM.
The degree was established in response to a demand from companies in the sector to enhance the knowledge acquired by students, and it was taught at the facilities of the Furniture and Wood Technology Centre, located in Yecla.

The Regional Association of Furniture and Wood Entrepreneurs of the Region of Murcia (AREMA) was formally established on 12 May 1977 under the name "Provincial Association of Carpentry, Cabinetmaking, and Various Trades." Since then, it has been dedicated to defending the interests of entrepreneurs involved in the manufacture of furniture, upholstery, general carpentry, and related sectors in this Autonomous Community.

The AREMA Annual Award has been presented since 2015 to recognise work, effort, support, and career achievements linked to the furniture and wood sector. Typically, the award ceremony takes place at an event during the Yecla Furniture Fair.

Gothic sculpture in Murcia is scarce due to history, social peculiarities, and heritage preservation. After the Reconquista, the transformation of Muslim temples into Christian ones and the introduction of figurative sculpture were gradual processes. Though limited in number, existing medieval sculptures in Murcia are mainly religious, and the lack of knowledge about authors and workshops highlights the modernity of the concept of authorship.
In the era of the Murcian Renaissance, sculpture focuses on religious and devotional works, with wood being the predominant medium in Spain.
The Renaissance altarpiece in the Church of Santiago in Jumilla, stands out for its architectural design and round sculpture, influenced by both classical and Iberian elements.
The works of the Master Builder Jerónimo Quijano found in the Cathedral of Murcia, show clear Italian influences.
During the 16th century, altarpieces become prominent artistic expressions in Murcia, with the workshop of the Bautista Estangueta family taking center stage.
During the Baroque period, spanning the 17th and 18th centuries, wood carving experienced a notable boom in Spain.

This era witnessed the creation of numerous masterpieces of religious sculpture, many of which are still found in churches and cathedrals in the Region of Murcia. Murcian Baroque sculptors significantly contributed to this movement, leaving a lasting legacy in the form of skillfully carved devotional images and altarpieces.
In the first Murcian Baroque period, the scarcity of local sculptors often led to the hiring of professionals from other regions, with a notable demand for workshops from Andalusia.

In the early years of the 17th century, sculptors such as Cristóbal de Salazar and Juan Sánchez Cordobés worked in Murcia, but their works exhibited a certain rigidity and were still anchored in Renaissance classicism.
Nicolás de Bussy, established in 1688, marked a turning point towards the Baroque, influencing Murcian sculpture.

By the late 17th century, the "Baroque splendor" began to manifest in Murcia. Nicolás Salzillo, arriving from Naples, along with artists like Antonio Dupar, introduced new Baroque forms into Murcian sculpture. Dupar's work demonstrated a transition towards more energetic and dynamic forms, anticipating the "Salzillesco" style that would characterize Murcian sculpture.

In 1727, the second generation of the Salzillo family, led by Francisco Salzillo, established family workshops that would produce internationally recognized works. Technically exquisite and aesthetically pleasing, Salzillo's sculptures brought a new aesthetic concept to devotional art. By the late 18th century, Salzillo's name was already respected, but his working style remained true to the artisanal character, with a workshop employing multiple hands in the creative process.

After the end of the Baroque period, sculpture in the Western world follows the path of new ideas, known in Art History as Neoclassical, which impose themselves on artistic forms and aesthetic tastes.

The preference for classical canons resurfaces progressively, and the ideas of Baroque sculptors or perennial references are questioned or debated. However, sculpture experiences a significant recession in production and aesthetic interest throughout Europe. In contrast to painting, sculpture suffers from a lack of research and reflection proportionally.

In Murcia, after the dominant influence of Francisco Salzillo, sculpture becomes practically nonexistent, beyond devotional commissions. Although Neoclassicism and historical Romanticism influence sculptural aesthetics in Spain and Europe, seeking to create archetypes rather than copying the ancient, there is hardly any trace of Neoclassicism in Murcia. Despite political and philosophical changes in the West, Murcian sculpture remains focused on the religious.

During the latter half of the 19th century, sculpture in Murcia continues to be primarily devotional, with followers of Salzillo such as Francisco Sánchez Tapia, Sánchez Araciel, Dorado Brisa, Ramiro Trigueros, Julio Delgado, and Rafael Asensi.
In this era, design gains relevance, paving the way for the exploration of new materials and forms in contemporary sculpture.
The idea emerges that sculpture is no longer limited to extracting the desired object from the material; instead, design and collaboration with specialized craftsmen set the tone.

Although Murcian sculptors may not be immersed in the artistic debates of the time, the 20th century brings about a revolution in industrial activity that impacts craftsmanship. New materials take precedence, challenging academic principles regarding the nobility of materials. While craftsmanship persists in certain regional areas, the difficulty of keeping up with new artistic trends, such as cubism, is reflected in Murcian sculpture.

José Planes and Juan González Moreno represent a new opportunity for Murcian sculpture in the 20th century. Although González Moreno excels mainly in works of religious imagery, his interest in contemporary Italian sculptors like Manzù and Martini positions him as a versatile sculptor, exploring noble materials and showing interest in the profane.
The shadow of Francisco Salzillo persists, and although some sculptors from Murcia, such as Planes, explore new currents, religious themes remain predominant until the 1960s and 1970s.

In the decades of the 1960s and 1970s, artists like Pedro Pardo and Elisa Seiquer introduce works that mark an advancement for Murcian sculpture. Although they do not embrace international avant-garde themes, their contribution is crucial in a local context rooted in traditional tastes.
Today, wood carving in the Region of Murcia remains a vibrant form of artistic expression, enriched by the historical legacy of master carvers and adapting to changing aesthetic sensibilities.
